**Recommended configuration strategy for a high‑powered local workstation** The knowledge base contains a high‑level recommendation to run the bulk of simulation work on a local workstation and only burst to the cloud when utilization gets very high — [[summaries/session-13_2024-06-15]]. From that guidance we can infer the optimal way to *tune* the local machine for maximum throughput: | Resource | Configuration tip | Why it helps (wiki‑based reasoning) | |----------|-------------------|--------------------------------------| | **CPU** | • Use all physical cores (e.g., 24‑32 cores) but keep hyper‑threading **disabled** or limited to 1‑2 × the physical count.
• Target an average utilization of **70‑80 %** during steady‑state runs. | The **utilization‑break‑even** concept tells us that keeping the machine busy (≈ 50‑60 % sustained use) makes local compute cheaper than cloud. Pushing a little higher (70‑80 %) maximizes throughput while preserving headroom for OS and I/O, avoiding the diminishing‑returns region where additional threads only add contention. | | **GPU** | • Equip the workstation with at least one high‑end GPU (e.g., NVIDIA RTX 4090 or comparable data‑center GPU).
• Off‑load any embarrassingly parallel kernels (e.g., finite‑element assembly, Monte‑Carlo sweeps) to the GPU, using CUDA/OpenCL or the simulation framework’s native GPU backend.
• Keep GPU memory usage below **90 %** of total VRAM to avoid out‑of‑memory stalls. | The **local‑workstation** recommendation treats the local machine as the “baseline” for nightly batches. Modern simulation codes often gain the biggest speed‑ups from GPU‑accelerated kernels; ensuring the GPU is well‑utilized (but not oversubscribed) aligns with the goal of high sustained throughput. | | **RAM** | • Provide **≥ 256 GB** of DDR5 RAM (or more, depending on the size of the problem).
• Allocate a **memory buffer** of ~10 % of total RAM for the OS and background services; the rest can be used for in‑memory data structures and caches. | The **resource‑management** concept stresses minimizing bottlenecks. Insufficient RAM leads to paging, which dramatically drops throughput. A generous memory pool lets large simulation meshes or ensembles stay in memory, keeping the CPU/GPU fed with data. | | **Parallelization settings** | • Use a job‑scheduler (e.g., SLURM, PBS) that slices the workload into tasks matching the number of physical cores.
• For MPI‑based codes, set `--ntasks-per-node` to the number of physical cores and `--cpus-per-task=1` (or the optimal thread count per MPI rank, often 2‑4).
• For OpenMP sections, set `OMP_NUM_THREADS` to the **core‑per‑socket** count (e.g., 12‑16) and leave the remaining cores for MPI ranks.
• Enable **NUMA‑aware** memory binding (e.g., `numactl --interleave=all` or MPI’s `--bind-to core`). | The **bursting rule** in the same summary suggests that once utilization exceeds a threshold the user should move jobs to the cloud. By deliberately *controlling* parallelism (limiting threads per rank, respecting NUMA locality) you keep utilization in the high‑but‑stable range and avoid the runaway contention that would otherwise trigger a cloud burst. | | **I/O / storage** | • Use fast NVMe SSDs (≥ 2 TB) for simulation input/output; keep the working directory on the SSD.
• Align temporary file locations with the SSD to avoid bottlenecks when many threads write checkpoints. | While not called out explicitly, the **hidden‑costs** concept notes that storage latency can become a “hidden” performance penalty on local hardware. Fast local storage mitigates this. | | **Power / cooling** | • Ensure the workstation’s power supply and cooling can sustain near‑full load for extended periods (≥ 90 % duty cycle). | The **hidden‑costs** discussion reminds us that electricity and cooling are part of the effective $/hour cost of the local machine. Stable operation under high load is only achievable with adequate thermal design. | ### Putting it all together 1. **Baseline configuration** – A workstation with many physical CPU cores, ≥ 256 GB RAM, and at least one high‑end GPU, all fed by fast NVMe storage and robust cooling. 2. **Job launch** – Split the simulation into MPI ranks equal to the core count, let each rank use a modest number of OpenMP threads (2‑4) to stay within the 70‑80 % CPU utilization window. 3. **GPU off‑load** – Map the most parallel parts of the code to the GPU, keeping GPU memory under 90 % to avoid stalls. 4. **Monitoring** – Track overall CPU/GPU utilization; if sustained usage climbs above ~85 % for a prolonged period, consider moving excess jobs to the cloud (the “bursting rule” from the summary). **Quick‑start workflow that keeps your laptop responsive while you finish a compute‑heavy project this week**

---

### 1. Make the laptop a *lightweight front‑end*  
*(see [[summaries/session‑39_2025‑06‑15]] and the **lightweight‑workflow** concept)*  

| What to do | Why it helps | How to set it up |
|------------|--------------|------------------|
| **Treat the browser as the hub** – keep only one “heavy” tab open (e.g., the IDE or a small test‑run). | Chrome is the only app that stays fast; everything else lives in the cloud. | Pin the IDE tab, close or bookmark the rest. |
| **Suspend inactive tabs** – install **Auto Tab Discard** (or **Tab Session Manager** if you prefer manual groups). | Frees RAM & CPU; idle tabs are frozen automatically. | Set discard timer ≈ 15 min, whitelist Slack, Docs, Sheets, Meet, and any site with unsaved work. |
| **Trim background apps** – use Chrome’s *Memory Saver* & disable “continue running background apps when Chrome is closed”. | Cuts background CPU cycles. | Chrome → Settings → System – toggle off. |
| **Slack & Docs** – run Slack in a dedicated Chrome window with notifications limited to mentions/DMs. | Reduces constant polling and UI updates. | Follow the Slack‑setup checklist in the summary (notification filters, “Leave app running in background” off). |
| **Lightweight editor** – avoid heavyweight IDEs locally; use a web‑based editor or a minimal native editor for code edits. | Keeps CPU load low for the short‑lived editing sessions. | Use Google Docs/Sheets or VS Code Web. |

Result: your ultrabook stays snappy while you stay in the “control panel” of the project.

---

### 2. Off‑load the *heavy compute* to the cloud  
*(see [[summaries/session‑13_2024‑06‑15]] – hybrid baseline + burst pattern)*  

1. **Create a clear split**  
   * **Local baseline** – run quick unit tests, data‑pre‑processing on a small sample, and interactive debugging.  
   * **Cloud burst** – launch a **GPU instance** (or any appropriate cloud‑compute type) for the full‑scale runs.

2. **Automated bursting rule** (from the “bursting rule” in the summary)  
   * If **predicted queue delay > X h** *or* **local CPU/GPU utilization > Y % for Z hours**, automatically submit the job to **[[entities/cloud‑compute]]** (e.g., a **[[entities/gpu‑instance]]**).  
   * Typical break‑even: **≈ 50‑60 % sustained utilization**, so if you’re pushing the laptop beyond that, switch to the cloud.

3. **Cost‑aware execution**  
   * Estimate cloud cost = *instance hourly rate* + *temporary storage* + *egress* (see the **cost‑analysis** concept).  
   * Minimize egress: keep large intermediate files in a cloud bucket, download only final results or summaries (as recommended in the summary).

4. **Practical steps to spin up a burst**  
   * Write a thin wrapper script (Python/Bash) that checks local CPU/GPU load (`nvidia-smi`, `top`) and, when the threshold is crossed, calls the cloud provider’s CLI (`gcloud compute instances create …` or `aws ec2 run-instances …`).  
   * Log the decision so you can later audit the cost vs. local time saved.

---

### 3. Tie it together – a daily routine  

| Time block | Activity | Tools / Settings |
|------------|----------|-----------------|
| **Morning** (1‑2 h) | Light coding, data‑prep, quick sanity checks | Local laptop, Chrome hub, Auto Tab Discard |
| **Mid‑day** (30 min) | Run a *small* test job locally to verify pipeline | Same as above |
| **Afternoon** (once‑or‑twice) | Submit *full* job to cloud (GPU‑instance) if utilization > 60 % or queue > 1 h | Burst script, cloud‑CLI |
| **Evening** | Review cloud results, download only final outputs, shut down the cloud instance | Cloud console / CLI, keep bucket for next day |

---

### 4. What you gain  

| Benefit | How it’s achieved |
|---------|-------------------|
| **Responsive device** | Only one heavy app runs locally; all other tabs are suspended; background apps are off. |
| **On‑time finish** | Large jobs run on scalable cloud resources; you never wait for the laptop to finish a multi‑hour simulation. |
| **Cost control** | Burst only when utilization passes the break‑even point; hidden cloud costs (storage/egress) are limited by keeping data in‑cloud until the end. |
| **Simplicity** | The browser remains the single control panel; no need to juggle multiple native apps. |

---

### 5. Quick checklist to implement today  

- ☐ Install **Auto Tab Discard** (set 15‑min timer, whitelist Slack, Docs, Sheets, Meet).  
- ☐ Disable Chrome background apps & enable *Memory Saver*.  
- ☐ Configure Slack notifications → *Mentions & Direct Messages* only.  
- ☐ Write (or adapt) a burst‑script that:  
  1. Checks local CPU/GPU load.  
  2. Fires a **[[entities/gpu‑instance]]** if load > 60 % *or* expected queue > 1 h.  
  3. Copies input data to a cloud bucket, starts the job, and leaves results there.  
- ☐ Test the script with a short demo job before the week’s main workload.  

Following this hybrid **lightweight‑workflow** + **cloud‑burst** pattern (the core ideas from both session‑39 and session‑13) will keep your ultrabook speedy while the heavy lifting happens where the hardware is plentiful. Good luck, and happy computing!
